sections.body: Citation mapping and discovery is the work of turning the record of who cites whom into something a reader can actually navigate. In practice this means building citation graphs from metadata, grouping papers by what they say rather than only by shared references, and classifying the intent behind each citation. Systems now do this at scale: a single query can pull the neighbourhood of a paper, show which later works lean on it, and surface papers that sit between two fields. This site holds 295 research papers in its library, so the graphs here are small enough to inspect by hand and large enough to show real structure. The output is not a verdict on quality, it is a map of attention and lineage.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The mechanical parts are largely solved. Citation extraction, deduplication, and graph construction work well on clean metadata, and embedding based clustering reliably separates papers that share a topic from papers that merely share a venue. What remains hard is intent. A citation can support, dispute, reuse a method, or appear only because a reviewer asked for it, and automatic classifiers still confuse these, especially in short reference lists. Trend forecasting is the weakest area, because citation counts lag publication by years and early signals are noisy. Coverage is also uneven, since fields with weak indexing or non English output are underrepresented in any graph built from mainstream sources.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The five pages here move from structure to prediction. Citation Graphs Over Time gives the base layer, showing how links accumulate and how a paper's position shifts as later work arrives. Clustering Papers by Meaning takes the same corpus and regroups it by content, which is what you want when the citation links are too sparse to be useful. How a Paper Is Cited zooms in on a single edge and asks what kind of use it represents, so it is the page for judging influence rather than counting it. Bridge Studies Between Fields sits at the intersections the clusters reveal, for readers tracking work that belongs to two communities at once. Forecasting Research Trends closes the section by asking what the graph implies about where attention is heading, with the caveat that the signal is always behind the present.
